title: The Mobilisation Gap: What a New Mining Services Contract Costs Before the First Invoice Lands
linkedin:
Winning a new contract is supposed to be the good news. For a lot of mining services contractors, it's also the moment cash gets tightest.

Crew recruitment, plant mobilisation, inductions, insurances, sometimes a performance bond. All of it has to be paid before a single hour is billed.

Payment terms then kick in. Thirty to sixty days from a certified invoice is standard across the sector, and that invoice usually can't be raised until a full period of verified work has been delivered.

Stack mobilisation spend against that payment lag and the gap between the first dollar out and the first dollar in can run past two months, on a contract that is comfortably profitable on paper from day one.

That's the part that catches good operators off guard. The margin is real, the client is reputable, and the business still ends up negotiating an overdraft extension or delaying a supplier payment, not because the work is unprofitable but because the cash hasn't caught up with the ledger yet.

The contractors who avoid this treat mobilisation cash as something to negotiate into the contract itself. An upfront mobilisation payment. Fortnightly progress claims instead of monthly. Or simply knowing the number well enough to arrange a facility before the gap opens, not during it.

Retention adds another layer, often five to ten percent of every claim held back until practical completion. Run two or three contracts at once and that's real money sitting outside the business's control for months.

If your business works in mining and resources services, you'll know the feeling of winning a new contract and then finding the next month or two tighter than expected. It's a pattern we see often with contractors across Queensland's resources corridors.

The costs of starting a new job, crew recruitment, plant mobilisation, inductions, insurances and sometimes a performance bond, all land before a single hour is billed. Mining companies and head contractors then typically take thirty to sixty days to pay from a certified invoice, and that invoice often can't be raised until a full period of verified work has been delivered.

Stack those together and a contract that's genuinely profitable can still create a real cash squeeze in the weeks after it starts. Add retention money held back until practical completion, and that pressure can run even longer on a business managing several contracts at once.

None of this means the contract wasn't worth winning. It usually means the cash timing was never modelled before the tender was signed. If you're currently mobilising for a new contract or bidding on one, it's worth working out that number in advance rather than discovering it mid-project.
